result.summary: Glaucus swims from Sicily to Circe's halls and asks for a charm to make Scylla love him. Circe offers herself instead, he refuses, and in jealous anger she poisons Scylla's bathing bay and turns her lower body into barking dogs. Scylla later becomes a rock that sailors avoid.

scenes.title: Glaucus swims to Circe
scenes.summary: Glaucus passes Ætna, Zancle and Rhegium and swims through the Etrurian seas to Circe's halls.
scenes.stakes: Glaucus risks lasting unrequited longing for Scylla.

scenes.title: Glaucus asks, Circe offers herself
scenes.summary: Glaucus begs for a charm against Scylla's scorn. Circe offers her own love, and he swears he will never change while Scylla lives.
scenes.stakes: Glaucus's hope of winning Scylla; Circe's pride and desire are at risk.

scenes.title: Scylla is transformed
scenes.summary: Circe brews herbs, walks over the waves to Rhegium and poisons Scylla's bay. Scylla is turned into a monster with dogs about her loins, then later into a rock.
scenes.stakes: Scylla loses her human form and eventually her life as a woman.

alias_notes.explanation: Circe is called this as a child of the Sun, whom Ovid also calls Titan.

notable_quotes.reason: Glaucus's vivid vow of constancy using impossible images.

analysis.text: Rejected love turns to jealousy and cruelty. Circe punishes the rival instead of the man who refused her.
The tale explains the dangerous Strait of Messina, linking Scylla's rock to Homeric sailing lore.

legacy.text: Scylla, with Charybdis, gave English the phrase 'between Scylla and Charybdis' for a choice between two dangers.

fun_facts.text: Ovid here links Scylla to Ulysses' voyage, drawing on Homer's Odyssey.

language_notes.text: "Eubœan plougher of the waves" refers to Glaucus, a fisherman from Anthedon in Eubœa who became a sea-god; the periphrasis replaces his name.
Ætna lies on the Giant's jaws: the giant Typhœus (or Enceladus) was said to be buried beneath the volcano.
Ausonian means Italian; Ausonia was an old poetic name for Italy. The strait described is between Italy and Sicily.
Glaucus was transformed by eating a magic herb, which turned him into a sea-god. Circe's herb-lore makes him think she can help.
The Sun saw Venus with Mars and exposed them, so Venus punished his descendants with unhappy loves. Circe is the Sun's daughter.
Hecate was the goddess of magic and the night, invoked in sorcery.
"Cerberean" means like Cerberus, the three-headed dog guarding the underworld.
In the Odyssey, Scylla seized six of Ulysses' crew as his ship passed her rock.

context_notes.text: Circe was a sorceress who lived on an island and turned visitors into beasts, hence the wild animals filling her halls.
The sun at midday casts the shortest shadows, so Scylla rests in the bay at noon to escape the heat.
Scylla's rock stood in the strait near Charybdis and was a notorious danger to sailors, so it was avoided.

literary_notes.text: Glaucus lists impossibilities, trees in the sea and seaweed on mountains, to show his love can never change.
Circe's conflicting feelings, love for Glaucus and rage at his rival, show her passion turning toward cruelty.
The gradual horror of Scylla discovering the barking dogs, and carrying what she flees, makes the transformation vivid.
